- The third experiment (low S, high cat) maintained M7 as the leading model, but M2 and M13 are still closely following. The fact that M7 still fits well even at low substrate concentrations suggests it might either be the true mechanism or possesses enough parameter flexibility to mimic the `cat` dependent interactions of M2/M13.
- My aim for the previous turn was partially achieved: we separated the models further, but the top cluster (M7, M2, M13) remains somewhat entangled. 
- The aim for this turn is to definitively separate mechanisms dependent on free catalyst (`cat`) from those dependent on the catalyst-substrate complex (`catS`).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To cleanly distinguish between the remaining top candidates, we should run an experiment at the maximum substrate concentration (S = 5.0) and the maximum catalyst concentration (cat = 0.2), with no initial product. 
At S = 5.0, the system will be heavily saturated, rapidly driving almost all free `cat` into the `catS` intermediate state. This will strongly suppress mechanisms that rely on interactions between free catalyst molecules, such as catalyst dimerization (M2: `2cat<=>cat2`) or bimolecular free catalyst deactivation (M13: `2cat=>inactive`), because the concentration of free `cat` will be depleted. 
Conversely, this condition will massively amplify mechanisms that depend on `catS`. For M7 (`S+catS<=>catS2`), the high S will force the formation of the inhibitory `catS2` complex. For M18 (`2catS=>inactive`), the high concentration of `catS` (approaching 0.2) will cause rapid second-order deactivation. For M16 (`S+catS=>inactive`), the combination of high S and high `catS` will also trigger rapid deactivation. By shifting the dominant catalyst species from free `cat` (as in Exp 3) to `catS` (in this proposed Exp 4), we will orthogonally probe the system and break the degeneracy between the M2/M13 cluster and the M7/M16/M18 cluster.
</hypothesis>
